en.title: Netflix's Below: Is This Newfoundland Creature Feature Your Next Widow's Bay?
en.summary: A taut new Netflix miniseries drops anchor in a remote Newfoundland community, unleashing Lovecraftian horrors and corporate greed. With Josh Hartnett leading the charge, this creature feature promises a deeply original, culturally authentic, and *fun* binge.
en.body:
Forget the typical summer blockbuster; Netflix's latest offering, **Below**, is poised to become your next obsession, harkening back to the atmospheric charm and monstrous dread of **Widow's Bay**. This taut six-episode miniseries, set to premiere on October 8, 2026, plunges viewers into the quirky, close-knit community of Snook's Arm, Newfoundland, a real-life locale that grounds the fantastical elements with striking cultural authenticity. Creator **Jesse McKeown** masterfully weaves a tale that’s as much about the human condition as it is about the terrifying, mysterious aquatic lifeforms threatening its existence.

At the heart of **Below** is **Calvin Penney**, portrayed with compelling depth by **Josh Hartnett**. We witness Calvin’s childhood trauma, a tragic incident involving his family home and the unforgiving sea, which casts a long shadow over his adult life. Now struggling with the economic fallout of climate change and pollution impacting the local ice harvesting industry, Calvin’s latest catch hints at something far more sinister lurking beneath the waves. This discovery attracts the attention of local scientist **Fonda Howander**, played by **Mackenzie Davis**, who begins to unravel the unsettling truth. The series masterfully balances the external threat of the unknown creature with the internal anxieties of a community grappling with environmental and societal pressures, creating a unique brand of horror that feels both fresh and deeply resonant.

## The Monster and the Message

The series draws comparisons to **The Meg** for its looming, colossal threat, but **Below** carves its own path by focusing on the unique ecosystem and the specific anxieties of its Newfoundland setting. **McKeown**’s decision to value character development as much as the central predicament ensures that the six episodes feel tight and purposeful, avoiding the narrative bloat that plagues so many streaming series. The show’s commitment to bright, naturalistic cinematography, a rarity in the genre, further enhances its distinctiveness. It’s a creature feature that doesn’t shy away from its environmental message, using the encroaching monstrosity as a potent metaphor for the destructive forces of corporate greed and ecological neglect, all while remaining *goofily entertaining* and memorably quirky.

## What Fans Are Saying

Early buzz suggests **Below** is poised to capture the imaginations of fans who fell in love with the specific blend of isolation, mystery, and creeping dread found in **Widow's Bay**. The emphasis on a lived-in community, coupled with the introduction of Lovecraftian elements, promises a narrative that is both intellectually stimulating and viscerally thrilling. Viewers are particularly excited about the strong ensemble cast, including **Charlie Heaton**, and the potential for a show that respects its audience's intelligence while delivering genuine scares and compelling thematic depth. The series’ brief, focused run is also being celebrated as a welcome antidote to streaming fatigue, offering a complete and satisfying arc without unnecessary padding.

## What's Next

With its October 8, 2026 release date on the horizon, **Below** is shaping up to be a must-watch event for fans of intelligent creature features and character-driven thrillers. Keep an eye out for further details regarding the full cast and specific plot reveals as the premiere approaches.

content_raw: If Widow’s Bay had added a kraken to its menagerie of the monstrous and the ghoulish, it might’ve looked something like Below . Like that Apple TV breakout, this taut Netflix miniseries captures the quirky personalities of a remote island community, but intertwines them with Lovecraftian monsters from the deep for a clever creature feature that launches a tale of climate change and corporate greed from a rock-solid dock of cultural authenticity. Anchored by a strong Josh Hartnett performance, it’s a show with a message that also never forgets to be goofily entertaining and memorably quirky. Creator Jesse McKeown values his characters as much as their predicament, leading to six episodes that make for a fun hang, even if their relative briefness leaves you wanting more. Then again, in the age of streaming bloat, a Netflix series that’s not only free of the typical plot sag but mostly shot in the bright sunlight feels as rare and awe-inspiring as the mysterious aquatic lifeforms at the center of Below . Hartnett stars as Calvin Penney, an ice harvester in the Newfoundland village of Snook’s Arm, a real place off the coast of Canada that was resettled in 2018. Below opens with a young Calvin watching the Penney family home being moved across the water from one seaside location to another, only for it to get caught on something . His dad jumps from the boat to the floating abode, a choice that ends in a tragedy that will haunt Calvin for decades. Years later, and struggling to make ends meet due to the impact of climate change and pollution, Calvin’s latest haul seems dirty and somehow off, hinting at something unusual happening in the waters off Snook’s Arm. This catches the attention of a local scientist named Fonda Howander (Mackenzie Davis), who begins to examine what almost appears like a new amoebic presence in the ice. And that’s all before a massive iceberg appears on the horizon. McKeown and his writers populate Snook’s Arm with memorable characters, most of them related to Calvin. There’s his supportive and headstrong sister Ruth, played by Newfoundlander Willow Kean, who adds some welcome local flavor to a cast who put on some entertaining but broad Canadian accents that sound like most of their research consisted of watching multiple episodes of Shoresy . There’s also the next generation of Penneys: Calvin’s daughter Mary (Ruby Stokes) and his sons Jay (Rohan Campbell) and Wade (Charlie Heaton). They all get subplots impacted by the main arc of the show, including a love interest who Mary brings home to meet the family and some debts that could get Jay in physical trouble. Of course, Stranger Things vet Heaton gets the most screen time, and he leans into a very different role than the one that made him famous, playing Wade as a goofy risk-taker who probably wouldn’t give soft-spoken Hawkins loner Jonathan Byers the time of day.
